title: Chapter 32: The Morning Dew 5
content:
Chapter 32

This time, Wei Wuxian didn’t sleep a wink. He lay wide awake, counting the seconds until just before five in the morning. When the dull ache in his limbs finally eased and feeling returned to his fingers, he didn't waste a heartbeat. Sliding smoothly beneath the covers, he stripped off his robes and tossed them unceremoniously onto the floorboards.

Then, reaching over, he undid Lan Wangji’s sash and peeled the man's inner layer down.

Originally, he’d planned to strip him clean to the waist, but catching sight of the mottled brand resting right below Lan Wangji's collarbone made his fingers freeze. The memory of those horrific discipline scars scored across his back flashed unbidden in his mind. A sudden twinge of unease pricked his chest; he reached out, intending to pull the collar closed and cover him back up.

That second of hesitation was his undoing.

Feeling the chilly draft against his bare chest, Lan Wangji stirred, his brow pinching slightly as his eyelashes fluttered open.

The moment his eyes focused, he rolled straight off the mattress, hitting the floorboards.

To be fair, no one could fault the peerless Hanguang-jun for a momentary lapse in his legendary composure. When a man wakes up from a dead-drunk stupor to find another man lying half-naked beside him, his own robes wrenched down to his elbows, and both of them tangled skin-to-skin beneath the same blanket—dignity tends to take a backseat.

Wei Wuxian held the quilt up to his chest, strategically leaving one bare, smooth shoulder exposed.

Lan Wangji stared from the floor, breathless. "You..."

Wei Wuxian let out a sleepy, nasal hum. "Mm?"

Lan Wangji’s voice faltered. "Last night, I..."

Propping his chin in one hand, Wei Wuxian threw him a cheeky wink, his smile practically dripping with mock intrigue. "Last night, Hanguang-jun? You were wild."

Lan Wangji sat frozen in petrified silence.

"Don't tell me," Wei Wuxian teased, tilting his head. "You don't remember a single thing?"

Judging by how the blood drained straight from Lan Wangji's face, he was genuinely drawing a total blank.

Good. If he actually remembered waking up and tailing him into the woods to catch him summoning Wen Ning, things would be a hundred times messier. Lying would blow up in his face; telling the truth would be sheer suicide.

After blowing his cover and shooting himself in the foot so many times, Wei Wuxian finally felt like he’d reclaimed a scrap of his old swagger. He’d won a round. Part of him wanted to press the advantage, but if he ever wanted to trick Lan Wangji into drinking with him again, he couldn't leave the man permanently traumatized.

Knowing when to fold, Wei Wuxian kicked the quilt aside, proudly displaying his neatly laced trousers and boots. "Look at you, clutching your virtue! Relax, Hanguang-jun. I only stripped our layers for a laugh. Your honor is entirely intact. You haven't been defiled, I promise."

Lan Wangji remained frozen on the floor. Before he could squeeze out a syllable, the sharp clatter of shattered porcelain cracked through the room.

The noise was painfully familiar. Down on the low table, the Evil-Quelling Qiankun pouches were having another violent fit, knocking over the tea set—only this time, with all three pieces under one roof, the thrashing was three times more frantic. Between one man dead-drunk and the other wrung dry, their nightly duet ofResthad completely slipped through the cracks.

Worrying Lan Wangji might lash out in pure panic and accidentally run him through right there on the bedsheets, Wei Wuxian scrambled up. "Business! Duty calls, Hanguang-jun. Let's handle this first."

He threw his robes over his shoulders, rolled out of bed, and offered a hand to the man standing by the floor. He meant to haul him up, but bare-chested and disheveled, the lunge looked alarmingly like he was diving to rip the rest of Lan Wangji’s clothes off. Still rattled, Lan Wangji stepped back on reflex. His heel caught on an obstacle, throwing him off balance; looking down, he found Bichen resting by his boots, where it had been dropped the night before.

Across the room, the drawstring had worked itself loose. A pale, vein-riddled hand had already wormed its way halfway out of the mouth of the pouch. Wei Wuxian slipped a hand into Lan Wangji’s half-open collar, rummaging around until his fingers closed around the smooth bamboo flute.

"Don't look so terrified, Hanguang-jun," he teased, pulling the instrument free. "I'm not trying to take liberties. You swiped my flute last night, remember? I'm just taking it back."

To add insult to injury, he even smoothed Lan Wangji’s lapels over his shoulders and neatly knotted his sash for him.

Lan Wangji stared back with an unreadable, deeply conflicted look, clearly burning to interrogate him about what else had transpired during his blackout. But habit died hard; forcing himself to prioritize the emergency, he swallowed his questions, composed his expression, and summoned his seven-stringed guqin.

Three pouches lay on the table: one holding the left arm, one the legs, and the last containing the newly excavated torso. Together, they made up the bulk of a complete corpse. Feeding off one another's proximity, their resentment surged exponentially. The air grew stifling, far deadlier than before, forcing the pair to play three full movements ofRestback-to-back before the thrashing finally subsided.

Wei Wuxian tucked the flute into his sash. Just as he stepped forward to gather the scattered remains, his eyes caught on the open casket. "Well, well. Our dear friend was quite the looker, wasn't he?"

The silk burial shroud draped across the torso had slipped aside, exposing a broad, chiseled chest. The waist was lean, the abdominal muscles sculpted with clean, devastating definition—a powerhouse physique without an ounce of bloat, the kind of build most martial artists would give their right arm for.

Wei Wuxian looked it up and down, so impressed he actually reached out and gave the abs a couple of solid smacks. "Look at this, Hanguang-jun! If this fellow were still breathing, a strike like that would probably snap my wrist from the rebound alone. What kind of regimen produces this?"

The corner of Lan Wangji’s brow gave a faint, violent twitch. He didn't answer.

When Wei Wuxian casually slapped the chest two more times, Lan Wangji finally snapped. Marching forward with a completely blank face, he snatched the empty pouches and began packing the limbs away in stony silence.

Wei Wuxian took a step back, letting him work. Within moments, Lan Wangji had crammed every severed piece into the silk, tying off the drawstrings with half a dozen aggressive, airtight knots.

Unbothered, Wei Wuxian looked down at his own borrowed frame, gave his ribs an unimpressed poke, and tied his sash, making himself look halfway presentable again.

Catching Lan Wangji’s gaze darting his way, heavy with unspoken hesitation, Wei Wuxian leaned in with a sly grin. "Why the stare, Hanguang-jun? Still sweating it? Trust me, I didn't lay a finger on you last night—and for the record, you didn't touch me either."

Lan Wangji hesitated, as if wrestling with an internal demon, before dropping his voice low: "Last night... aside from taking your flute... did I...?"

"You?" Wei Wuxian cut in breezily. "Wondering what else you got up to? Nothing scandalous, really. You just talked. A lot."

Lan Wangji’s throat bobbed, the pale line of his neck tightening. "...What did I say?"

"Oh, nothing earth-shattering. Just, you know... how much you love..."

Lan Wangji’s stare turned entirely rigid.

"...how much you love rabbits."

Lan Wangji shut his eyes tight and turned his head away.

Wei Wuxian offered a patronizing, soothing pat in the air. "It's fine! Bunnies are adorable—who doesn't love them? I love them too! Love them roasted with chili, hahahaha! Come on, Hanguang-jun. You drank so much last night—well, not much, but you got so utterly plastered—you must be feeling it this morning. Wash your face, have some tea, and rest up. We'll head out once you're steady. The compass is pointing southwest this time. I'll pop downstairs to grab some breakfast so you can have some peace."

Turning toward the door, a flat, frigid command caught his heels: "Wait."

Wei Wuxian looked over his shoulder. "Yeah?"

Lan Wangji pinned him with a long, unblinking stare. Finally, he spoke: "Do you have money?"

Wei Wuxian grinned from ear to ear. "Of course I do! As if I don't know where you keep your purse. Don't worry, I'll bring yours back up. Take your time, Hanguang-jun, no rush at all!"

Stepping into the corridor and pulling the door shut behind him, Wei Wuxian slumped against the wall, doubled over in silent, breathless wheezing.

Lan Wangji seemed deeply rattled by the whole ordeal, locking himself in the room and refusing to show his face for quite some time. Waiting on him, Wei Wuxian ambled downstairs, strolled through the market stalls, picked up some steamed buns, and sat on the inn's front steps, munching lazily while soaking in the morning sun.

Before long, a pack of boys around thirteen or fourteen came tearing down the street.

The kid in the lead sprinted like the wind, clutching a spool of string. Bobbing high on the draft above his head was a large, round kite. The boys trailing behind brandished crude wooden toy bows, hollering at the top of their lungs as they loosed tiny blunt arrows into the air, trying to shoot it down.

Watching them, a fond warmth touched Wei Wuxian’s chest. Archery was a mandatory art for disciples of every great clan, but boys their age were allergic to static target drills. Aside from loose beasts on night-hunts, shooting down kites was everyone's favorite pastime. Each shooter launched a kite, and whoever flew the highest, drifted the farthest, and still managed to skewer the center won the round. It had started as a friendly contest among the younger generation of cultivators, but the trend had soon trickled down to common street children—though their clumsy toy arrows lacked the lethal punch of real spiritual fletching.

Back in Lotus Pier, Wei Wuxian had dominated kite-shooting with the Jiang disciples, sweeping first place almost every time. Jiang Cheng was perpetually stuck in second: his kite either drifted too far for his arrows to reach, or when his shot hit true, it was never as high as Wei Wuxian's. Their kites were a solid ring larger than anyone else's, shaped like soaring, mythical beasts, painted in lavish, screaming colors with gaping maws and jagged, fluttering tails dancing on the wind. Viewed from the ground, they looked remarkably alive—less terrifying and more wonderfully clumsy. Jiang Fengmian had personally whittled the bamboo frames for them, and Jiang Yanli had painted the silk by hand. Every time they took those kites out to the docks, they walked with their chins held high.

The memory tugged the corners of Wei Wuxian’s lips into a soft smile. Craning his neck, he squinted up at the children's kite. It was painted a brilliant, shimmering gold, crafted into an enormous, featureless circle.

What on earth is that supposed to be?he wondered.A flatbread? Or some weird monster I’ve never heard of?

A sudden gust swept down the lane. Flying low between the cramped rooftops, the golden circle lost its lift and plummeted straight into the dirt.

One of the boys wailed, "Oh no! The sun fell down!"

Everything clicked. The kids were re-enacting the Sunshot Campaign.

This was Yueyang, not far from the borders of Qishan. Back during the peak of the Qishan Wen Clan's tyrannical reign, their disciples had thrown their weight around unchecked, and the local townsfolk had suffered through hell—either terrorized by neglected spirit beasts or bullied by arrogant Wen cultivators. After the Sunshot Campaign crushed the clan, toppling their centuries-old dynasty in a blink, the border towns had erupted into jubilant celebrations that eventually hardened into local tradition. Games like this were merely the living echo of that relief.

Dropping their bows, the children huddled in a circle, scratching their heads in deep debate: "What do we do? It hit the ground before anyone even shot it! Who gets to be the boss now?"

A boy shot his hand up. "Me, obviously! I'm Jin Guangyao—I'm the one who slit the throat of the big Wen villain!"

Perched on the steps, Wei Wuxian watched the performance with thorough amusement.

In a game like this, Lianfang-zun—the current Chief Cultivator riding high on the world's praise—was naturally the most coveted role. People might sneer at his shady parentage behind closed doors, but that humble rise only made his ascension look all the more dazzling. Spending years deep undercover in the belly of the beast, playing the entire Qishan Wen Clan like a fiddle while leaking state secrets left and right; then riding the post-war wave with peerless charm, sharp diplomacy, and ruthless maneuvering straight to the throne of the cultivation world—his journey was nothing short of legendary. If Wei Wuxian were playing, he’d pick Jin Guangyao too. Crown the kid, totally fair!

Another boy bristled in protest. "No way! I'm Nie Mingjue! I won the most battles and took the most prisoners! I'm the leader!"

"Jin Guangyao" shot back, "Yeah, but I'm the Chief Cultivator!"

"Nie Mingjue" raised a pudgy fist. "Chief Cultivator my foot! You're still my Third Brother! See me on the street and you'll tuck your tail between your legs and run!"

True to his role, "Jin Guangyao" immediately hunched his shoulders and skittered away in theatrical terror.

A third boy scoffed, "You died young, you big corpse!"

Since picking a hero usually meant admiring the man, "Nie Mingjue" took the jab personally. "Jin Zixuan, you dropped dead way before I did! You're even more of a ghost!"

"Jin Zixuan" crossed his arms, huffing, "So what if I died early? I'm ranked third on the beauty charts!"

"Third place only counts for your face, pretty boy!"

Just then, a child who looked worn out from the running shuffled over to the steps, dropping down beside Wei Wuxian. Waving a dismissive hand like a tired diplomat, he muttered, "Alright, knock it off, both of you. I'm the Yiling Patriarch. I'm the strongest one here. I'll make the sacrifice and take the crown."

Wei Wuxian stared at him.

Glancing down, he noticed a short, whittled twig tucked into the boy's waistband. Chenqing, apparently.

Leave it to children to ignore moral posturing and judge a man purely by his combat stats, happily crowning the Yiling Patriarch based on raw firepower alone.

Another kid stomped forward. "Wrong! I'm the Sandu Shengshou! I'm the deadliest!"

"The Yiling Patriarch" gave him a deeply unimpressed look. "Come on, Jiang Cheng. When have you ever beaten me? You lose every single round—how can you say you're the strongest with a straight face? Have some shame!"

"Jiang Cheng" sneered, "I lose to you? Do you even remember how you died?!"

The faint smile on Wei Wuxian’s lips vanished in a heartbeat.

It felt as though a needle dipped in venom had struck him out of nowhere, sending a dull, icy ache pulsing through his marrow.

Beside him, the little "Yiling Patriarch" jumped up, clapping his hands with manic glee. "Look at me! Chenqing in my left hand, Tiger Tally in my right, and the Ghost General at my back! I'm completely invincible! Hahahahaha!"

Brandishing his wooden stick in one hand and raising a jagged garden stone in the other, he laughed like a maniac. "Where's Wen Ning?! Fall in!"

A timid boy in the back raised a shy hand, squeaking, "I'm... I'm over here. But, uh... during the Sunshot Campaign... I wasn't dead yet..."

Wei Wuxian felt it was time to step in.

"Excuse me, esteemed Sect Leaders," he called out. "May I ask a question?"

The kids froze. Adults usually yelled at them to clear the street; none of them had ever been questioned with this level of deadpan, formal gravity.

"The Yiling Patriarch" eyed him warily. "What do you want?"

Wei Wuxian asked, "Where are the cultivators from the Gusu Lan Clan?"

"Right there."

"Where?"

The boy pointed a finger toward a quiet child who hadn't uttered a single syllable since the game began. "That one."

Wei Wuxian looked over. The boy was exceptionally pretty, blessed with clean, delicate features, wearing a scrap of white hemp rope tied neatly around his forehead to serve as a ribbon.

"And who is he supposed to be?" Wei Wuxian asked.

The boy scowled in disdain. "Lan Wangji!"

...Fair enough. They had nailed the character down to the bone. To play Lan Wangji, keeping your mouth shut was step one!

Without warning, the corners of Wei Wuxian’s lips pulled upward again.

The venomous needle seemed to dissolve into thin air, the phantom pain sweeping clean away. He muttered to himself with a soft chuckle:Remarkable. How does such a boring, stiff block of wood manage to make me this happy every single time?

When Lan Wangji finally descended the stairs, he stepped into the sunlight only to find Wei Wuxian perched on the steps, surrounded by a flock of children happily splitting steamed buns.

Munching on his food, Wei Wuxian was actively directing two boys posed back-to-back: "...Now, picture ten thousand elite Wen cultivators surrounding you, armed to the teeth, hemming you in on all sides! Sharp eyes! Fierce! Good, just like that. Lan Wangji, pay attention: you aren't your usual polite self right now—you're covered in blood! Radiating pure murder! Eyes cold as ice! Wei Wuxian, step closer to him. Can you twirl a flute? Let me see you spin it. One-handed. Put some swagger into it! Do you know what swagger is? Here, hand it over, let me show you."

The little "Wei Wuxian" nodded obediently, handing over the wooden stick. Wei Wuxian took the twig between two fingers, flicking his wrist until the wood became a dizzying blur, prompting breathless gasps of awe from the huddled audience.

Lan Wangji stood on the threshold, speechless.

As he stepped down the stairs, Wei Wuxian noticed his approach, dusted off the seat of his trousers, and waved a cheery goodbye to the kids. Scrambling to his feet, he fell into step beside Lan Wangji, chuckling relentlessly as they walked, looking for all the world like he’d been hit with laughing poison.

Lan Wangji walked on in stoic silence.

"Hahahahaha, I'm so sorry, Hanguang-jun!" Wei Wuxian wheezed, wiping a tear from his eye. "I gave your breakfast to the kids. I'll buy you another set down the road!"

"Mn."

"Come on, weren't those two adorable? Guess who the kid with the rope around his forehead was pretending to be? Hahahahaha!"

Lan Wangji walked several paces in heavy silence before he finally cracked, his voice dropping into a tight, suspicious whisper: "...What else did I do last night?"

It couldn't be that simple. Why else would the man be laughing this hard?!

Wei Wuxian waved his hands frantically. "Nothing, nothing, nothing! You didn't do a thing! I'm just amusing myself, hahahaha... Alright, cough, Hanguang-jun, let's talk business."

"Speak," Lan Wangji replied, steadying his stride.

Slipping into professional focus, Wei Wuxian reasoned, "The coffin-battering in the Chang cemetery lay dormant for ten full years, only to wake up the second we arrived. That's no coincidence. Something triggered it."

"What do you believe the trigger was?"

"Sharp question," Wei Wuxian nodded. "I believe the trigger was that torso being dug up."

"Mn."

Lan Wangji’s listening face was so intensely solemn that it instantly reminded Wei Wuxian of him drunkenly clutching his two fingers the night before. Fighting off another wave of hysterical laughter, he cleared his throat. "Dismembering a body isn't just about bloody revenge—it's a sinister method of spiritual suppression. Whoever chopped him up deliberately planted the pieces in areas plagued by anomalous malice."

"Fighting poison with poison," Lan Wangji noted. "Maintaining equilibrium through mutual restraint."

"Exactly," Wei Wuxian said. "The moment that gravedigger unearthed the torso yesterday, the ward keeping the Chang spirits down collapsed, and the coffin-battering started up again. It mirrors the exact system the Qinghe Nie Clan used in their blade vault to balance the sabre spirits against the corpses in the walls. For all we know, the culprit lifted the technique straight from the Nie Clan's blueprints. Which means this person shares deep, intimate ties with both Qinghe Nie and Gusu Lan. Definitely not a small-timer."

"There are very few who fit that description," Lan Wangji murmured.

"Yeah. The net is tightening," Wei Wuxian agreed. "Besides, the fact that they're scrambling to relocate the body proves they're panicking. They're going to make another move soon. Even if we don't hunt them down, they'll come knocking on our door. And the more moves they make, the more tracks they leave behind. Not to mention, our dear friend's hand will keep pointing the way. Still, we need to pick up the pace—only the right arm and the head remain. We have to beat them to the punch."

Heading southwest, the pair pressed forward. This time, the severed left hand guided them toward the mist-shrouded valleys of Eastern Shu—pointing straight toward a haunted settlement that locals dared not name: a city of the dead.
